text: The same information can be laid out in two shapes. In long format, each row is one observation — one city, one month, one amount. In wide format, each row is an entity, and categories spread across columns — one row per city with a column for each month. Databases and most plotting and modeling tools prefer long; human-readable reports prefer wide. Reshaping is how you move between the two, and you'll do it constantly.

Merge the illustrative orders and customers tables together, then add a month column pulled from the order date using dot-d-t dot month. That gives us one tidy table to reshape every which way for the rest of this lesson.

Pivot underscore table groups rows by an index, spreads another column across the columns, and aggregates the values. Pivot by city down the side and status across the top, summing amount — Austin shows 45 returned and 630.49 shipped. Read it like an Excel PivotTable. A NaN means no orders existed for that combination at all. But watch Denver's pending cell — it shows 0.0, not NaN, because a pending order does exist there, its amount is just missing, and sum treats a missing value as 0. That same reading-with-care habit from the groupby lesson applies here too.

Pass aggfunc as mean, count, or even a list like sum and count together. Fill underscore value equals 0 replaces the NaN cells outright. And margins equals True adds an All row and column of totals — pivoting city by month with margins, the bottom row reads 255.49, 385.25, and 259.99, which matches the resample results from the dates lesson exactly, a great sanity check. Notice Denver's All cell shows NaN even though its month-2 cell shows 0.00 — both come from that one missing amount, and the two cells disagree, so treat totals for groups with missing data with real suspicion.

When you just want counts of combinations, crosstab is shorter than pivot underscore table. Crosstab of city against status shows Austin with 1 returned and 3 shipped, Boston with 1 cancelled and 2 shipped, and Denver with 1 pending.

Pivot rearranges values without summarizing, so each index-and-column combination must appear only once. First build a tidy monthly table with groupby, then pivot it wide by city and month. But try to pivot the raw orders by city and status directly, and pandas refuses with a ValueError — duplicate entries, cannot reshape — because Austin has three shipped orders, and pivot has no way to decide which amount should fill that one cell. Pivot underscore table resolves duplicates with aggfunc; plain pivot can't, so when in doubt, reach for pivot underscore table instead.

Melt is the reverse move. Id underscore vars names the columns to keep as identifiers, and every other column gets stacked into two new ones. Take a wide table of quarterly sales per customer, with columns q1 and q2, and melt it, keeping customer underscore id as the identifier, naming the stacked columns quarter and sales. The result has one row per customer per quarter — exactly the long format that groupby, plotting libraries, and scikit-learn generally want.

So here's how to pick the right tool. Pivot underscore table when you need to summarize into a grid. Plain pivot when every combination is already unique and you just want to reshape. Crosstab when all you need is quick counts of combinations. And melt when you need to turn a wide, spreadsheet-style export back into long format.

To recap: long tables have one observation per row; wide tables spread categories across columns. Use pivot underscore table to summarize into a grid and handle duplicates, pivot when each combination is unique, crosstab for counts, and melt to return to long format.
